newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH DOCTORS TO START GO-SLOW PROTEST ON TUESDAY.
newsitem.headline: POLISH DOCTORS TO START GO-SLOW PROTEST ON TUESDAY.

text.p: A strike committee of Polish doctors decided to step up on Tuesday a three-week-old pay and funding protest by lavishing extra-meticulous care and costly drugs on patients and abiding by all possible regulations.
PAP news agency reported leaders of an all-Poland doctors' union strike committee, who met late on Friday in the central town of Bydgoszcz, as saying the protest so far proved ineffective.

"We now want to start an 'Italian strike' for an indefinite period of time...this way we want to exert economic pressure on the government," PAP quoted Jacek Wutzow, deputy head of the union, the OZZL, as saying.
So far doctors have mainly refrained from fulfilling certain administrative paperwork and issuing medical leave certificates.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski was unruffled by the prospect of an extended protest, PAP news agency reported.
"I think the statement that the strike will mean we are at last going to be examined properly is the best news we could have heard from medical circles," it quoted him as saying.
"I'm going to go for a check-up," he said, urging reporters to do the same.

The union launched its partial strike at hospitals and clinics around the country in early December after reaching deadlock in talks with the government. Doctors cancelled some routine examinations and operations, while continuing to treat emergency and life-threatening cases.
The doctors' union has excluded cancer, psychiatric, children's and maternity wards from the stoppage, but its action has been criticised by some doctors. The Solidarity union has stood aside.
The doctors want budget spending on the health service to rise to six percent of gross domestic product this year, while the government plans to allocate 4.5 percent.
They seek a collective wage deal, for doctors only, which would increase their monthly salaries to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) -- three times the average industrial wage.
The health ministry argues that it does not have the resources to meet the doctors' pay demands but has boosted 1997 budget spending on health by a real 10 percent over 1996.

It also says a health insurance reform now passing through parliament, setting up new special funds that will allocate money to hospitals according to their efficiency, will eventually benefit medical staff and the whole system.
